units.title: Scarcity and Opportunity Cost
units.tip: Economics exists because resources are limited but wants are unlimited. Scarcity forces choices. Opportunity cost is what you give up by choosing one thing over another. Every decision has a trade-off.

exercises.question: What is scarcity in economics?
exercises.answer: Limited resources cannot satisfy unlimited wants
exercises.explain: There is never enough of everything for everyone. Land, labor, time, and money are all scarce. Scarcity is why economics exists.
choices: Limited resources cannot satisfy unlimited wants
A shortage of one specific good
When a store runs out of inventory

exercises.question: Is scarcity a problem for wealthy people?
exercises.answer: Yes, even the wealthy face scarcity of time
exercises.explain: No matter how rich you are, you have only 24 hours a day. Time is scarce for everyone. Money is less scarce for the rich but still finite.
choices: Scarcity does not exist for large economies
Yes, even the wealthy face scarcity of time
No, scarcity only affects poor people

exercises.question: What are the three basic economic resources?
exercises.answer: Land, labor, and capital
exercises.explain: Land includes natural resources. Labor is human effort. Capital is tools, buildings, and equipment used to produce. All three are scarce.

exercises.question: Because of scarcity, what must every economy decide?
exercises.answer: What to produce, how to produce it, and who gets the output
exercises.explain: With limited resources, every economy answers these three questions. Different systems answer them differently.
choices: What to produce, how to produce it, and who gets the output

exercises.question: Can any economy eliminate scarcity completely?
exercises.answer: No, scarcity is a fundamental economic reality
exercises.explain: Even the richest countries face scarcity. Resources are always limited relative to wants. This is why choice matters.
choices: No, scarcity is a fundamental economic reality

exercises.question: What is opportunity cost?
exercises.answer: The value of the next best alternative you give up
exercises.explain: If you choose college over working, the opportunity cost is the wages you do not earn. Every choice has a cost: the path not taken.
choices: The time it takes to decide
The total cost of a purchase
The value of the next best alternative you give up

exercises.question: You have 2 hours and can either study or work. Work pays 20 dollars per hour. What is the opportunity cost of studying?
exercises.answer: 40 dollars in forgone wages
exercises.explain: By studying, you give up 2 hours of work at 20 dollars per hour, totaling 40 dollars. That is your opportunity cost.
choices: You do not have an opportunity cost

exercises.question: Is opportunity cost the same for everyone?
exercises.answer: No, it depends on individual circumstances and alternatives
exercises.explain: A student giving up study time to work faces different opportunity costs than a professional. Your options shape your costs.
choices: No, it depends on individual circumstances and alternatives
Yes, it is the same for everyone
Only skilled workers have opportunity costs

exercises.question: What is a trade-off?
exercises.answer: Giving up some of one thing to get some of another
exercises.explain: You cannot have everything, so you trade. More spending on A means less on B. A trade-off shows a choice has costs.
choices: Buying two items at the same time
Giving up some of one thing to get some of another

exercises.question: A company uses a factory to make cars. If they used the same factory for trucks instead, the opportunity cost is:
exercises.answer: The cars they would have made
exercises.explain: Choosing to make trucks means giving up car production. The cars not made are the opportunity cost of that choice.
choices: The cars they would have made
The money spent on the factory

units.title: Supply and Demand
units.tip: Supply is how much sellers are willing to offer. Demand is how much buyers want. The price adjusts until supply equals demand, creating market equilibrium. When demand rises or supply falls, prices go up.

exercises.question: What is demand in economics?
exercises.answer: The quantity of a good people want to buy at each price
exercises.explain: Demand curves show the relationship: lower prices mean more people want to buy, higher prices mean fewer buyers.
choices: The quantity of a good people want to buy at each price

exercises.question: What is supply in economics?
exercises.answer: The quantity of a good sellers are willing to offer at each price
exercises.explain: Supply curves show: lower prices mean sellers offer less, higher prices encourage more production.
choices: The quantity of a good sellers are willing to offer at each price

exercises.question: What happens to demand when a product becomes trendy?
exercises.answer: Demand increases, people want to buy more
exercises.explain: A trend makes a product more desirable. At every price, more people now want it. The demand curve shifts right.
choices: Demand increases, people want to buy more

exercises.question: What happens to demand for umbrellas during a drought?
exercises.answer: Demand decreases because fewer people need them
exercises.explain: Without rain, umbrellas are less useful. People want fewer of them at every price. Demand shifts left.
choices: Demand decreases because fewer people need them

exercises.question: A factory's production capacity increases. What happens to supply?
exercises.answer: Supply increases, more can be produced at each price
exercises.explain: More capacity means sellers can offer more product without raising prices. The supply curve shifts right.
choices: Supply increases, more can be produced at each price

exercises.question: What is market equilibrium?
exercises.answer: The price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
exercises.explain: At equilibrium, sellers want to provide exactly what buyers want to buy. There is no shortage or surplus. The market clears.
choices: The price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded

exercises.question: What happens when demand exceeds supply?
exercises.answer: There is a shortage, and prices tend to rise
exercises.explain: More buyers want the good than sellers supply. The shortage causes prices to increase, encouraging more supply and less demand.
choices: There is a shortage, and prices tend to rise

exercises.question: What happens when supply exceeds demand?
exercises.answer: There is a surplus, and prices tend to fall
exercises.explain: Sellers have more than buyers want. A surplus pushes prices down, encouraging more buyers and less production.
choices: There is a surplus, and prices tend to fall

exercises.question: How do prices guide the economy toward equilibrium?
exercises.answer: Rising prices encourage more supply and less demand; falling prices do the opposite
exercises.explain: Prices are signals. Shortages raise prices, attracting more producers and fewer buyers until balance is reached.
choices: Rising prices encourage more supply and less demand; falling prices do the opposite

exercises.question: If the market price is below what it costs sellers to produce, what do sellers do?
exercises.answer: Sellers reduce supply or leave the market
exercises.explain: When the price will not cover costs or give a reasonable profit, sellers cut production or exit, which pushes the price back up.
choices: Sellers reduce supply or leave the market

units.title: Elasticity and Sensitivity
units.tip: Elasticity measures how responsive quantity demanded or supplied is to price changes. Some goods are elastic (demand drops sharply when price rises), others are inelastic (demand barely changes). Understanding elasticity explains why price increases hurt some industries more than others.

exercises.question: What is price elasticity of demand?
exercises.answer: How much the quantity demanded changes when price changes
exercises.explain: Elasticity measures responsiveness. A 10% price increase causes a 5% quantity drop for one good, a 20% drop for another.
choices: How much the quantity demanded changes when price changes
The highest price anyone will pay

exercises.question: What is an 'elastic' demand?
exercises.answer: Quantity demanded changes a lot when price changes
exercises.explain: Elastic goods are price-sensitive. A small price increase causes many buyers to switch or buy less. Examples often include restaurant meals and entertainment.
choices: Quantity demanded changes a lot when price changes

exercises.question: What is an 'inelastic' demand?
exercises.answer: Quantity demanded changes very little when price changes
exercises.explain: Inelastic goods are not price-sensitive. Buyers need them regardless of cost. Examples: insulin, gasoline (short-term).
choices: Quantity demanded changes very little when price changes

exercises.question: If medicine is inelastic and price rises, what happens?
exercises.answer: Quantity demanded falls only slightly; total revenue likely increases
exercises.explain: People need medicine whether the price is high or low. A price increase reduces quantity little, so total revenue goes up.
choices: Quantity demanded falls only slightly; total revenue likely increases

exercises.question: Why are luxury goods typically elastic in demand?
exercises.answer: People can choose not to buy them when prices rise
exercises.explain: Luxury items are not essential. When a restaurant raises prices, people eat out less, choosing home cooking instead.
choices: People can choose not to buy them when prices rise

lessons.title: Price Elasticity of Supply and Cross-elasticity

exercises.question: What is price elasticity of supply?
exercises.answer: How much quantity supplied changes when price changes
exercises.explain: Supply elasticity measures seller responsiveness. Some goods can be produced faster when profitable; others take time.
choices: How much quantity supplied changes when price changes

exercises.question: Why is agricultural supply often inelastic?
exercises.answer: Crops take months to grow; farmers cannot quickly increase production
exercises.explain: Wheat planted now harvests in months. A sudden price rise does not cause next week's harvest to double.
choices: Crops take months to grow; farmers cannot quickly increase production

exercises.question: Why is manufacturing supply more elastic than agriculture?
exercises.answer: Factories can increase production quickly by adding shifts or workers
exercises.explain: A factory can shift to higher capacity in weeks or days. Farmers cannot speed crop growth.
choices: Factories can increase production quickly by adding shifts or workers

exercises.question: What is cross-price elasticity?
exercises.answer: How demand for one good changes when the price of another good changes
exercises.explain: If butter becomes expensive, less butter is bought and more margarine is bought. The two goods are substitutes.
choices: How demand for one good changes when the price of another good changes

exercises.question: Cheese and crackers are complements. If cheese prices rise, what happens to crackers?
exercises.answer: Cracker demand falls because fewer people buy the cheese-cracker combo
exercises.explain: Complements are used together. When cheese gets more expensive, people buy less cheese, and demand for crackers falls too.
choices: Cracker demand falls because fewer people buy the cheese-cracker combo

units.title: Market Structures
units.tip: Markets vary based on the number of sellers and how much power each has. Perfect competition has many sellers with no power. Monopoly has one seller controlling price. Oligopoly has a few large sellers who dominate. Structure shapes pricing power and innovation.

exercises.question: What is perfect competition?
exercises.answer: Many sellers offer identical products; no single seller controls price
exercises.explain: In perfect competition, each seller is tiny. If one raises price, buyers switch to another. It is an ideal case; some farm markets come close.
choices: Many sellers offer identical products; no single seller controls price

exercises.question: What is a monopoly?
exercises.answer: One seller with no significant competition
exercises.explain: A monopoly controls supply and can set prices high because buyers have nowhere else to go. Examples: local utility, patent holder.
choices: One seller with no significant competition

exercises.question: How does a perfect competitor set prices?
exercises.answer: They accept the market price or exit; they cannot raise prices without losing all customers
exercises.explain: In perfect competition, any seller trying to raise price above the market rate loses all customers to others.
choices: They set any price they want
They accept the market price or exit; they cannot raise prices without losing all customers
They raise prices to maximize profit

exercises.question: How does a monopolist set prices?
exercises.answer: They choose price and quantity to maximize profit; customers have no alternatives
exercises.explain: A monopolist has pricing power. They can raise prices knowing customers cannot go elsewhere.
choices: Price is set by perfect competition
They choose price and quantity to maximize profit; customers have no alternatives

exercises.question: Why might a monopoly feel less pressure to innovate than firms in a competitive market?
exercises.answer: Without competitors, it faces little threat of losing customers
exercises.explain: Competitive markets push firms to improve to keep customers. A monopoly can keep earning profit without that pressure, though some still innovate.
choices: It always innovates more than competitors
Without competitors, it faces little threat of losing customers

exercises.question: What is an oligopoly?
exercises.answer: A market with a few large sellers who dominate
exercises.explain: Oligopolies have a small number of major firms controlling most sales. Commercial aircraft manufacturing is a classic example.
choices: A market with a few large sellers who dominate

exercises.question: How do oligopolists influence prices?
exercises.answer: They have some pricing power but must consider competitor reactions
exercises.explain: If one oligopolist raises price, others might not, stealing customers. Oligopolists carefully set prices to avoid price wars.
choices: They have some pricing power but must consider competitor reactions

exercises.question: What is a 'price war'?
exercises.answer: Competitors repeatedly cut prices trying to undercut each other
exercises.explain: In price wars, each firm cuts prices to win customers, and everyone's profit drops. They can occur in industries with close rivals, such as airlines.
choices: Competitors repeatedly cut prices trying to undercut each other

exercises.question: Why might oligopolists avoid price wars?
exercises.answer: Price wars can shrink every firm's profit
exercises.explain: If all firms cut prices deeply, margins shrink for everyone. Firms in an oligopoly often prefer to compete on features and brand instead.
choices: There is no reason to avoid them
Customers do not like low prices
Price wars can shrink every firm's profit

exercises.question: What is 'product differentiation' in oligopoly?
exercises.answer: Making your product distinct so buyers see rivals' products as poorer substitutes
exercises.explain: Firms use brand loyalty, unique features, or marketing to stand apart. This reduces direct price competition and gives more room to set prices.
choices: Making your product distinct so buyers see rivals' products as poorer substitutes

units.title: GDP, Inflation, and Unemployment
units.tip: GDP measures total economic output. Inflation is the rise in average prices over time. Unemployment is the percentage of people wanting work who cannot find jobs. Together, these three metrics describe an economy's health.

exercises.question: What does GDP stand for?
exercises.answer: Gross Domestic Product
exercises.explain: GDP is the total value of final goods and services produced within a country in a given period, usually a year. It measures the size of an economy.

exercises.question: What does growing real GDP (adjusted for price changes) indicate?
exercises.answer: The economy is producing more goods and services
exercises.explain: Rising real GDP means more output is being produced. It usually goes along with more jobs and rising incomes, and is generally seen as a sign of economic health.
choices: The economy is producing more goods and services

exercises.question: What is inflation?
exercises.answer: A sustained increase in the average level of prices
exercises.explain: Inflation means your money buys less. A 3% inflation rate means prices are 3% higher than last year on average.
choices: A sustained increase in the average level of prices

exercises.question: If inflation is 5% and your salary stays the same, what happens?
exercises.answer: Your purchasing power falls by about 5%
exercises.explain: With 5% inflation, the same salary buys roughly 5% less (about 4.8% precisely). You are relatively poorer unless your pay rises too.
choices: Your purchasing power falls by about 5%
Your purchasing power stays the same

exercises.question: What is the unemployment rate?
exercises.answer: The percentage of people wanting work who cannot find jobs
exercises.explain: Unemployment measures joblessness. A 5% rate means 5 out of 100 people wanting work are jobless.
choices: The number of people not working
People who chose not to work
The percentage of people wanting work who cannot find jobs

exercises.question: What causes inflation?
exercises.answer: Too much money chasing too few goods, or rising production costs
exercises.explain: If spending grows faster than the supply of goods, buyers bid prices up. Or if costs of production rise across the economy, prices rise.
choices: A drop in the money supply
Too much money chasing too few goods, or rising production costs
Falling demand across the whole economy

exercises.question: Is inflation always bad?
exercises.answer: Low, stable, predictable inflation is generally tolerable; high or unexpected inflation does more harm
exercises.explain: Mild, predictable inflation is easy to plan around. High or unexpected inflation erodes savings and creates uncertainty.
choices: Low, stable, predictable inflation is generally tolerable; high or unexpected inflation does more harm

exercises.question: What is 'deflation'?
exercises.answer: A sustained decrease in the average level of prices
exercises.explain: Deflation is the opposite of inflation: prices fall over time. It sounds good, but it can discourage spending and harm growth.
choices: A sustained decrease in the average level of prices

exercises.question: When does unemployment typically rise?
exercises.answer: During recessions when GDP falls
exercises.explain: When the economy shrinks, businesses lay off workers. Unemployment and falling GDP move together.

exercises.question: What is 'stagflation'?
exercises.answer: High unemployment and high inflation happening simultaneously
exercises.explain: Stagflation is economic stagnation plus inflation. Growth stalls and joblessness is high while prices keep rising, which makes it a hard problem to solve.
choices: High unemployment and high inflation happening simultaneously

units.title: Trade and Comparative Advantage
units.tip: Comparative advantage explains why trade benefits both parties. Even if one country can produce everything more efficiently, both gain by specializing in what they do relatively best. Trade increases total production and living standards.

exercises.question: What is comparative advantage?
exercises.answer: The ability to produce something at a lower opportunity cost
exercises.explain: A country with a comparative advantage in wheat gives up less of other goods to make it than another country does. That lower opportunity cost is why trade makes sense.
choices: The ability to produce something at a lower opportunity cost
The ability to produce more of everything

exercises.question: Can two countries benefit from trade even if one is better at everything?
exercises.answer: Yes, if each specializes in their comparative advantage
exercises.explain: Country A might be better at both shoes and wheat. But if it has comparative advantage only in shoes, both gain if A makes shoes and B makes wheat.
choices: Yes, if each specializes in their comparative advantage
Only if they are equally productive
No, trade only helps the weaker country

exercises.question: What does specialization mean in trade?
exercises.answer: Each country focuses on what it does relatively best
exercises.explain: A country specializes by producing what gives it comparative advantage. This increases total production.
choices: Each country focuses on what it does relatively best

exercises.question: Why might a country import food even though it can produce it?
exercises.answer: Its resources earn more making other goods, so it gains by trading for food
exercises.explain: If a country gives up a lot of other output to grow food but makes software at a low opportunity cost, it gains by selling software and buying food.
choices: Its resources earn more making other goods, so it gains by trading for food

exercises.question: What does trade increase?
exercises.answer: Total production and both countries' living standards
exercises.explain: When countries specialize and trade, total output can rise. Both can then consume more than they could alone.
choices: Total production and both countries' living standards

exercises.question: What is an externality?
exercises.answer: A cost or benefit of production affecting people not involved in the transaction
exercises.explain: A factory's pollution affects neighboring residents. A vaccine benefits people who did not get vaccinated. These are externalities.
choices: A cost or benefit of production affecting people not involved in the transaction

exercises.question: What is a negative externality?
exercises.answer: A cost imposed on third parties without compensation
exercises.explain: Pollution, noise, and congestion are negative externalities. The producer does not pay for the harm caused.
choices: A cost imposed on third parties without compensation

exercises.question: What is a positive externality?
exercises.answer: A benefit received by third parties without paying
exercises.explain: Education benefits society beyond the student. A vaccinated person protects others. Positive externalities are free benefits to society.
choices: When everyone buys the same product
A benefit received by third parties without paying

exercises.question: Why is pollution an example of market failure?
exercises.answer: The price of goods does not include pollution costs; society pays, not the producer
exercises.explain: Markets work when prices reflect all costs. Pollution is not priced in, so too much is produced, harming society.
choices: Pollution does not exist in markets
The price of goods does not include pollution costs; society pays, not the producer

exercises.question: How can government address negative externalities?
exercises.answer: Tax or regulate the polluting activity to reduce it
exercises.explain: A tax on pollution makes producers pay for the harm, which internalizes the cost. Regulations limit the activity directly.
choices: Ignore them and let markets decide
Tax or regulate the polluting activity to reduce it
